eras.name: Time-sharing
eras.background: Computers ran one job at a time in batches, so programmers waited hours or days for results. Time-sharing let many users at terminals share one machine. Paging stretched its small memory, and virtual machines gave each user a computer of their own.

eras.name: Unix
eras.background: Multics showed what a large time-sharing system could do, but it took years to deliver. A few Bell Labs programmers built the far smaller Unix and rewrote it in C. Its source spread to universities, which kept extending it until researchers asked how much really had to run inside the kernel.

eras.name: Commodity PCs
eras.text: Free Unix and VMs on the PC
eras.background: Cheap PCs spread, but Unix source still came with a costly AT&T license. Linux gave the PC a free Unix-like kernel, built in the open. PCs became internet servers holding thousands of connections, and VMware made virtual machines run on a processor never designed for them.

eras.name: Cloud
eras.background: Cloud providers rented slices of large server fleets to many customers, so isolating them cheaply became essential. CPUs gained virtualization support, and Linux gained namespaces and cgroups. Linux also learned to run verified programs inside the kernel, so operators could change it without patching it.

nodes.label: Time-sharing
nodes.problem: Batch jobs came back hours or days later, which made debugging slow and frustrating.
nodes.idea: MIT's CTSS switches the CPU among users at terminals on timer interrupts, and a multilevel feedback queue favors short interactive jobs.
nodes.impact: Interactive computing proved practical, and MIT built Multics as its successor.

nodes.label: Virtual memory
nodes.problem: Programmers had to shuttle program pieces between small core memory and a drum by hand.
nodes.idea: Manchester's Atlas splits memory into pages and moves them to and from the drum automatically.
nodes.impact: Paging became standard in general-purpose computers, and gave each process an address space of its own.

nodes.label: Hierarchical file system
nodes.problem: CTSS kept each user's files in one flat directory, with no way to group them or share them selectively.
nodes.idea: Multics arranges files in a tree of directories named by paths, with an access control list on each.
nodes.impact: Unix kept the tree and its path names, and every major OS has used it since.

nodes.label: Virtual machines
nodes.problem: Testing a new operating system needed a whole machine to itself, often at night or on weekends.
nodes.idea: IBM's CP gives each user a virtual System/360 that runs its own OS, usually the single-user CMS.
nodes.impact: Several systems, test versions included, could share one machine, and it grew into IBM's VM/370.

nodes.label: Working sets
nodes.idea: Denning tracks the pages each program used recently, and runs a program only while that set fits in memory.
nodes.impact: Thrashing could be avoided, and later page replacement, Linux's LRU lists included, still approximates recent use.

from.why: Paging let many programs share memory, but with too many of them the machine spent its time paging.

nodes.label: Unix
nodes.idea: Thompson and Ritchie build a small system where fork and exec start processes, and files, devices and pipes share one interface.
nodes.impact: Rewritten in C, it moved easily to new machines, and its interface became POSIX, which Linux and macOS follow.

from.why: Bell Labs quit Multics, leaving its programmers without the interactive system they had used.
Supplied the tree of directories, which Unix kept in a far smaller system.

nodes.label: Microkernels
nodes.idea: CMU's Mach keeps only threads, address spaces and message passing in the kernel, and moves file systems and drivers to user processes.
nodes.impact: Mach's messages were slow, but it lives on inside the XNU kernel of macOS and iOS. L4 later showed messages could be fast, and seL4 was proved correct.

from.why: Unix kernels kept growing, and every driver and file system ran with full privilege.

nodes.label: Journaling
nodes.problem: After a crash, fsck had to scan the whole disk, which grew slower as disks grew.
nodes.idea: Xerox's Cedar records each metadata update in a log first, a trick borrowed from databases.
nodes.impact: Recovery became fast, and file systems such as ext4, XFS and NTFS adopted journaling.

nodes.label: Linux
nodes.idea: Torvalds writes a free Unix-like kernel for the PC, developed openly with helpers worldwide.
nodes.impact: Paired with GNU tools, it now runs Android, most internet companies' servers and every TOP500 supercomputer.

from.why: Unix source still required a costly AT&T license.

nodes.label: Log-structured FS
nodes.idea: Berkeley's Sprite LFS writes every change, data included, sequentially to a log that is the file system itself.
nodes.impact: Writing new copies instead of overwriting carried into NetApp's WAFL, ZFS and Btrfs, and suits flash, which cannot overwrite in place.

from.why: Journaling logged only metadata, and small data writes still seeked all over the disk.

nodes.label: Binary translation
nodes.idea: VMware rewrites guest kernel code as it runs and lets guest applications run directly on the CPU.
nodes.impact: Virtual machines returned on cheap x86 hardware, and VMware's ESX Server brought them to datacenters.

from.why: Mainframes trapped every privileged instruction, but some sensitive x86 instructions did not trap.

nodes.label: Event notification
nodes.problem: select and poll scan every watched descriptor on each call, so servers with many idle connections spent their CPU scanning.
nodes.idea: The kernel keeps each process's interest set and returns only the ready descriptors, as FreeBSD's kqueue and Linux's epoll do.
nodes.impact: Event loops such as nginx and libuv serve many connections per thread. Linux's io_uring later moved the I/O calls themselves onto shared rings.

nodes.label: Hardware virtualization
nodes.idea: Intel VT-x and AMD-V add a CPU mode where guest kernels run directly and sensitive operations exit to the hypervisor.
nodes.impact: Hypervisors became small, and Xen and KVM came to run the public clouds, including AWS's Firecracker.

from.why: Binary translation was complex, and every guest kernel path had to be rewritten.
Supplied a scheduler and memory manager, so KVM could run each VM as an ordinary process.

nodes.label: Containers
nodes.idea: Run apps isolated on one shared kernel, as FreeBSD jails and Solaris zones had. Docker added images that pack an app with its files.
nodes.impact: Containers became a common way to ship software, and Google's Kubernetes came to run them across clusters.

from.why: Each VM carries a full guest OS, which is heavy and slow to boot for one app.
Supplied namespaces and cgroups to isolate and limit groups of processes on one kernel.

nodes.label: eBPF
nodes.idea: Grow the BSD packet filter into a general in-kernel virtual machine. A verifier checks each program before it runs.
nodes.impact: Now used for fast networking, tracing and security tools, and through sched_ext even to replace the CPU scheduler.

from.why: Changing kernel behavior meant patches or modules, where one bug could crash production servers.

main.title: CMU 15-213: Introduction to Computer Systems
main.why: How C becomes machine code, and what memory, linking, processes and I/O look like to a program. In English.

main.title: MIT 6.1810: Operating System Engineering
main.why: Page tables, system calls, page faults, locking, thread switching and file systems, each built into the xv6 kernel in labs. In English.

main.title: Linux Kernel Internals: Processes
main.why: From LinuxThreads to NPTL, then task_struct, the process lifecycle, fork and context switches. In Mandarin.

main.title: The Linux Scheduler: a Decade of Wasted Cores
main.why: CFS load balancing across scheduling domains had bugs that left cores idle while threads waited, which the authors exposed with an online invariant checker.

further.title: An EEVDF CPU scheduler for Linux
Avoiding CPU Throttling in a Containerized Environment
Modernizing the Meta Ads Service With an Open-Source Kernel Scheduler
further.why: EEVDF regressed ads latency, so Meta wrote a sched_ext policy that splits CPUs into latency-critical and background pools.

further.title: ghOSt: Fast & Flexible User-Space Delegation of Linux Scheduling

main.title: Non-scalable locks are dangerous
main.why: Linux ticket spinlocks collapse under contention because each unlock invalidates every waiter's cached copy; a Markov model explains the collapse, and MCS locks avoid it.

main.title: Multi-generational LRU: the next generation
main.why: The active and inactive page lists often evicted the wrong pages, so MGLRU sorts pages into generations and reclaims from the oldest.

main.title: TMO: Transparent Memory Offloading in Datacenters
main.why: Much of datacenter memory sits cold, so TMO offloads it to compressed RAM or SSD and uses PSI to stop before applications slow down.

further.title: TPP: Transparent Page Placement for CXL-Enabled Tiered-Memory

main.title: A Scalable and Explicit Event Delivery Mechanism for UNIX
main.why: select() costs grow with every file descriptor a server watches, so this mechanism lets applications register interest once and dequeue only new events.

further.why: Disk reads and open() block nginx's event loop even with O_NONBLOCK, so Cloudflare moved them to thread pools.

main.title: Ringing in a new asynchronous I/O API
main.why: Linux AIO worked well only for direct I/O and could still block, so io_uring passes requests and completions through rings shared with the kernel.

main.title: PostgreSQL's fsync() surprise
main.why: PostgreSQL trusted fsync to report failed writes, but after a writeback error the kernel can drop the dirty pages and never report it.

main.title: File Systems Unfit as Distributed Storage Backends: Lessons from 10 Years of Ceph Evolution
main.why: Building on local file systems cost Ceph in transactions and metadata, so BlueStore writes to raw devices.

further.title: I/O Passthru: Upstreaming a flexible and efficient I/O Path in Linux

main.title: kvm: the Linux Virtual Machine Monitor
main.why: x86 virtualization extensions made simple hypervisors possible, so kvm adds a guest mode to Linux and runs each virtual machine as an ordinary process.

main.title: Firecracker: Lightweight Virtualization for Serverless Applications
main.why: Serverless needs isolation stronger than containers without the weight of full VMs, so Firecracker is a minimal virtual machine monitor on KVM.

main.title: Understanding Host Network Stack Overheads
main.why: Link speeds have outgrown what one core can process, and this study finds that copying data to the application now dominates the Linux stack's cost.

main.title: The eXpress Data Path: Fast Programmable Packet Processing in the Operating System Kernel
main.why: Kernel bypass is fast but gives up the kernel's safety and tools, so XDP runs verified BPF programs in the network driver before the stack.

main.title: The eBPF Runtime in the Linux Kernel
main.why: eBPF extends the kernel without modules, and this survey covers how programs are verified, compiled and attached to kernel hooks.
